noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: understand the E – Z naming system for geometric isomers and why it is necessary to use this when the cis- and trans - naming system breaks down

primer.text: A double bond does not spin, so a carbon-carbon pair of different groups freezes into two distinct spatial arrangements. This note builds geometric isomerism from that single fact: the cis / trans shorthand, the CIP priority rules behind the E / Z system, and the cases where cis / trans naming collapses and E / Z must take over.

lessons.title: Rotation locked, two isomers
lessons.opening: Geometric isomerism is born from a single physical fact: the pi bond will not let the two double-bonded carbons spin. Whatever groups sit on those carbons therefore hold their side of the molecule permanently, and two different arrangements become two different compounds.
keyPoints: The pi bond restricts rotation about the C=C axis, freezing the groups on each carbon in place.
Geometric isomerism needs two different groups on each carbon of the double bond.
Identical groups parked on one shared side mark the cis arrangement.
Identical groups parked across the C=C from each other mark the trans arrangement.
The two isomers share formula and connectivity but differ in spatial shape, so they are stereoisomers.

low.restatement: Because the double bond cannot twist, groups keep their side: same side is cis, opposite sides is trans, and both versions count as separate isomers when each carbon carries two different groups.
low.analogy: Two people handcuffed by joined wrists face each other or stand back-to-back; without free arms they cannot swap between the two poses.
low.examPointer: State the requirement before naming anything: two different groups on each alkene carbon - examiners award the mark for the condition, not the labels alone.

medium.restatement: Restricted rotation means bond breaking would be needed to interconvert the two arrangements, so cis and trans forms are isolable compounds with distinct melting points and dipole moments, not conformers.
medium.analogy: A revolving door versus a locked turnstile: single bonds spin freely like the door, while the pi-bonded pair is the turnstile that only opens by breaking the mechanism.
medium.examPointer: If asked to explain why isomerism exists, quote restricted rotation AND the two-different-groups condition - half the marks die when one half is omitted.

check.stem: Which structural feature causes restricted rotation in an alkene?

options.text: The pi component of the double bond
options.explanation: Tearing the sideways overlap is the only way to twist, so rotation is barred.

options.text: The sigma component of the double bond
options.explanation: Sigma bonds alone allow free rotation, as in alkanes.
Hydrogens are passengers, not the lock.

options.text: The length of the carbon chain
options.explanation: Chain length does not affect rotation about the double bond.

check.stem: What condition must each double-bonded carbon satisfy for geometric isomerism?

options.text: It must carry two different groups
options.explanation: Only then are same-side and opposite-side arrangements distinguishable.

options.text: It must carry two identical groups
options.explanation: Identical groups make one arrangement, so no pair of isomers exists.
A double-bonded carbon holds only two substituent positions.

options.text: It must carry a hydrogen atom
options.explanation: Hydrogen is common but not required - E / Z works without it.

check.stem: In which arrangement do the identical groups sit facing each other across the double bond?

options.explanation: Trans means across - the matching groups sit on opposing sides.
Cis means parked together on one side.
That is a conformational term for single bonds, not alkene geometry.
Not a stereochemical term in this course.

check.stem: But-2-ene and but-1-ene: which one shows geometric isomerism?

options.explanation: Each double-bonded carbon of but-2-ene carries H and CH3 - two different groups.
The first carbon of but-1-ene carries two hydrogens, so no pair of arrangements exists.
But-1-ene fails the two-different-groups test on its first carbon.
But-2-ene plainly passes the test.

check.stem: What relationship links the cis and trans forms of but-2-ene?

options.text: They are stereoisomers with the same molecular formula
options.explanation: Connectivity is identical; only the spatial arrangement differs.

options.text: They are different homologous series members
options.explanation: Both are C4H8 with the same backbone.

options.text: They are conformers interconverting at room temperature
options.explanation: Rotation is locked, so they cannot interconvert freely.
Isomers always share one formula.

check.stem: State the two conditions needed for geometric isomerism about a C=C bond.
check.modelAnswer: Rotation must be restricted by the double bond, and each alkene carbon must carry two different groups.

check.stem: Define the terms cis and trans with respect to alkene geometry.
check.modelAnswer: Cis describes the isomer whose matching groups share one side of the C=C; trans describes the isomer whose matching groups face each other across the C=C.

check.stem: Explain why 2-methylpropene shows no geometric isomerism.
check.modelAnswer: One alkene carbon carries two identical methyl groups, so swapping sides produces the same molecule - with only one possible arrangement, no geometric pair exists.

check.stem: Draw and label the two geometric isomers of but-2-ene and give each name.
check.modelAnswer: But-2-ene exists as cis-but-2-ene with both methyl groups parked on one side, and trans-but-2-ene with the methyl groups facing across the double bond.

lessons.title: The cis / trans rule and where it fails
lessons.opening: The cis / trans shorthand needs a hydrogen on each double-bonded carbon to make sense. Once both carbons carry only carbon-based groups, chemistry borrows the CIP priority ladder and the E / Z system, which sorts every alkene without exception.
keyPoints: The cis / trans labels work cleanly only when each alkene carbon carries one hydrogen.
2-methylpropene defeats cis / trans naming because one carbon holds two methyl groups.
CIP rules rank substituents by atomic number: the higher the number, the higher the priority.
Z (zusammen) parks the two higher-priority groups on one shared side of the C=C unit.
E (entgegen) parks the two higher-priority groups on opposing sides of the C=C unit.

low.restatement: If each alkene carbon has one H, call the shared-side isomer cis and the facing one trans; otherwise rank the groups by atomic number and read Z (shared side) or E (facing sides) off the top priorities.
low.analogy: Cis / trans is a nickname that only works inside one family; E / Z is the official passport that works for every alkene at the border.
low.examPointer: Write the priority ranking explicitly in the margin before labelling E or Z - the working is frequently worth a mark even when the label is right.

medium.restatement: Priority comparison is decided at the first atom of difference: compare the atoms directly bonded to each alkene carbon, and only walk outward along ties. Carbon-based groups outrank plain hydrogen because carbon's atomic number 6 beats hydrogen's 1.
medium.analogy: Priority ranking is a tournament seedings table: the biggest atomic number is the top seed, and ties are settled by the next layer of the bracket.
medium.examPointer: Halogen-containing alkenes are the classic trap: Br (35) beats Cl (17) beats any carbon group - check atomic numbers before labelling.

check.stem: Why does cis / trans naming break down for 2-methylpropene?

options.text: One alkene carbon carries two identical methyl groups
options.explanation: With no distinguishing pair, same-side versus opposite-side becomes meaningless.

options.text: The molecule contains no double bond
options.explanation: 2-methylpropene is plainly an alkene.
Chain length is irrelevant to naming rules.

options.text: Its groups carry no hydrogens at all
options.explanation: Each methyl does carry hydrogens; the problem is the identical pair.

check.stem: Under CIP rules, which criterion sets substituent priority?

options.text: Atomic number of the directly bonded atom
options.explanation: Higher atomic number wins the higher priority.
Bulk plays no role; only atomic number counts.
The rule is atomic number, not electronegativity.

options.text: Alphabetical order of the group name
options.explanation: Names are irrelevant to CIP ranking.

check.stem: An alkene parks its two highest-priority groups on one shared side. Its label is:

options.explanation: Zusammen - the top priorities park together on one side.
Entgegen - that label belongs to priorities facing across.
Cis only applies with hydrogens present on both carbons.
Trans has the same restriction as cis.

check.stem: For 1-bromo-2-chloropropene, which atom wins the priority contest on its carbon?

options.explanation: 35 outranks every atom bonded alongside it.
17 beats carbon but not bromine on the same carbon's contest.
Carbon's 6 is the lowest here except hydrogen.
Hydrogen's 1 is always last in these contests.

check.stem: Which compound can be named with cis / trans labels?

options.explanation: Each alkene carbon carries one H and one methyl group.
One carbon carries two methyls - cis / trans is undefined.
Neither alkene carbon carries a hydrogen.
Substituted carbons without the required hydrogens need E / Z.

check.stem: State what the letters E and Z stand for and what each labels.
check.modelAnswer: E is entgegen, the isomer whose two top-priority groups face each other across the C=C; Z is zusammen, the isomer whose two top-priority groups share one side.

check.stem: Recall the CIP priority rule used in the E / Z system.
check.modelAnswer: Substituents are ranked by the atomic number of the atom attached directly to the alkene carbon, the largest number taking the highest priority.

check.stem: Explain why the E / Z system succeeds wherever cis / trans naming fails.
check.modelAnswer: E / Z never mentions hydrogens - it ranks whatever groups are present by atomic number, so it still produces two distinct labels even when every substituent is carbon-based or halogen.

check.stem: Assign E or Z to the isomer of 1-bromo-2-chloropropene in which Br and Cl sit on opposite sides, showing the priority working.
check.modelAnswer: Priority on the first alkene carbon: Br (35) over H (1); on the second: Cl (17) over CH3 (6). With Br and Cl facing across the C=C, the two top priorities are separated, so the label is E.

lessons.title: Reading E / Z off drawn structures
lessons.opening: Examiners hand you a drawn alkene and ask for its E / Z name or the isomer's formula. The drill never changes: mark the priority winner on each carbon, then read the geometry. This lesson drills that read on substituted and functionalised examples.
keyPoints: On a drawn alkene, mark the highest-priority group attached to each of the two alkene carbons.
Winners sharing a side reads Z; winners facing across reads E.
Functional groups do not break the rule - rank their first atoms by atomic number as usual.
Pairs of drawn structures that differ only in E / Z arrangement are stereoisomers to name separately.
Always finish by checking each alkene carbon really carries two different groups before labelling.

low.restatement: Circle the winner on each alkene carbon, then look: winners together means Z, winners apart means E.
low.analogy: Two team captains standing on the same touchline make a Z; standing on opposite touchlines makes an E.
low.examPointer: Annotate the structure - a circled priority on each carbon shows the examiner the method even if the final letter slips.

medium.restatement: For drawn pairs labelled A and B, the question is asking you to name both stereoisomers separately; a single answer covering both loses the second mark, so treat each drawing as its own compound.
medium.analogy: Twin photographs of the same molecule are two passports, not one: each drawing needs its own E or Z stamp.
medium.examPointer: With O-containing groups remember oxygen's atomic number 8 outranks carbon's 6 - hydroxyl-bearing alkenes are a favourite E / Z trap.

check.stem: A drawn alkene has its two highest-priority substituents on opposite sides. Name it:

options.explanation: Entgegen - the priorities face across from each other.
Zusammen needs the priorities together.
Cis vocabulary does not apply to substituted pairs without hydrogens.
Trans labels need the one-H-each-carbon condition.

check.stem: In ranking CH2OH against CH3 on the same alkene carbon, which wins priority?

options.text: CH2OH, because its carbon is bonded to oxygen
options.explanation: The oxygen (8) outranks the hydrogens (1) at the first point of difference.
Frequency plays no part in CIP ranking.
The first point of difference breaks the tie immediately.
Size is irrelevant; atomic number decides.

check.stem: What must you verify before assigning E or Z to any drawn alkene?

options.text: That each alkene carbon carries two different groups
options.explanation: Without that condition there is only one arrangement and no label to give.
Saturated molecules cannot show alkene stereochemistry at all.
The E / Z system never requires hydrogens.

options.text: That the drawing is to scale
options.explanation: Geometry is read from the drawing's arrangement, not its scale.

check.stem: Two drawn structures differ only in which side one bromine-bearing group occupies. How should the pair be reported?

options.text: As two stereoisomers, one E and one Z
options.explanation: The pair differ in spatial arrangement only, so each gets its own label.
The drawings are different compounds - naming one loses the other.
Connectivity is identical, so they are stereo-, not structural, isomers.
Both drawings carry the same molecular formula.

check.stem: Which atom's atomic number decides priority at the first point of difference on a functionalised alkene carbon?

options.text: The atom directly bonded to the alkene carbon
options.explanation: First-layer atoms set the ranking before any deeper comparison.

options.text: The atom farthest along the chain
options.explanation: Comparison stops at the first difference; distance does not win.

options.text: The heaviest atom anywhere in the group
options.explanation: Only the first layer matters unless that layer ties.

options.text: The atom with the most bonds
options.explanation: Bond count is not the ranking key.

check.stem: State the two-line procedure for naming a drawn alkene in the E / Z system.
check.modelAnswer: Rank the groups on each alkene carbon by atomic number of the attached atom, then label Z if the two winners share a side and E if they sit opposite.

check.stem: Give the priority order of bromine, chlorine, the methyl group and hydrogen under CIP rules.
check.modelAnswer: Bromine (35) ranks above chlorine (17), which ranks above the methyl carbon (6), which ranks above hydrogen (1).

check.stem: Explain why 1-chloroprop-1-ene shows cis / trans isomerism while 1-bromo-2-chloropropene does not.
check.modelAnswer: In 1-chloroprop-1-ene each alkene carbon still carries one hydrogen, so the cis / trans labels have a reference point; in 1-bromo-2-chloropropene both alkene carbons lack a hydrogen, so only the priority-based E / Z system applies.

check.stem: A drawn pair shows 1-bromo-1-propen-2-ol with the OH-bearing carbon's hydrogen on opposite sides in the two drawings. Report each isomer's label.
check.modelAnswer: Rank each carbon: Br (35) over CH2OH's carbon (6) on one side; CH2OH's oxygen-bearing carbon (6) over CH3 (6, broken by the O at the next layer). The drawing with the top priorities parked together is Z and the one with them facing apart is E.

glossary.definition: Stereoisomerism arising from restricted rotation about a double bond, giving same-side and opposite-side arrangements.
The ranking rule that orders substituents by the atomic number of the atom bonded directly to each alkene carbon.
The alkene whose two top-priority groups occupy one shared side of the C=C unit (zusammen).
The alkene whose two top-priority groups occupy opposing sides across the C=C unit (entgegen).
